prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Roughly etched onto Brian's arm is a swastika tattoo. Brian's sinister-looking tattoo is etched into his skin . The 11-year-old says his 10-year-old friend Temashi spent two days "scratching" the image onto his skin with a match stick. It only hurt a little bit, said Brian, one of thousands of Zimbabwean children who have fled their ravaged homeland for what they hope will be a better life in South Africa. For Brian and his friend, the symbol of the swastika does not represent the horrors of Hitler and the Holocaust. Instead, they say the ominous jagged lines on their arms mean "Germans never surrender." It is a twisted interpretation that, however misguided, gives strength to Brian, marking him as a "man" and "someone who does not surrender," he said quietly in a soft voice.  Watch the boys explain what the tattoos mean to them » . Brian and his young compatriots from Zimbabwe are on their own in a new country. Charities such as Save the Children and UNICEF classify them as "unaccompanied minors," but those words do not begin to describe their situation. They endure unimaginable hardships traveling to South Africa by themselves or with small groups of friends. They hitch rides on trucks, trains and taxis. Brian and his friends told CNN that when they got to the South African border at Beitbridge authorities let them walk through without passports or other documents. They then made their way to the border town of Musina, where boys beg on the streets or work on farms, and girls seem to disappear into South African society. UNICEF representative Shantha Bloemen said many Zimbabwean girls either turn to prostitution or work as domestic servants. Nearly all of the children -- some younger than 10 -- leave Zimbabwe because they hope their life will be better in South Africa. They said hunger, non-functioning schools and poverty were the reasons they left. Many are orphans, while some have parents, but they all dislike Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe's regime -- a government that has left them with no choice but to abandon their homes and join the exodus south. A quarter of Zimbabwe's population has fled the country, mostly to neighboring South Africa, Botswana and Mozambique, humanitarian groups said. The United Nations and Save the Children, which has an office based in Musina, report there has been a troubling increase in the number of children under 18 years old who are making the risky journey south from their homes in Zimbabwe to South Africa in search of work and food. Social workers from Save the Children and UNICEF told CNN that in June, 175 Zimbabwean children came over the border illegally and alone. In November, 1,016 kids made the same perilous journey. The boys older than 16 hang around Musina, sleeping on the sidewalk by a sports stadium along with older homeless men. Their days are spent waiting in line, jostling alongside hundreds of Zimbabwean adults, trying to apply for political asylum at a makeshift center opened by South African authorities. A South African official who processes asylum applications says it is common for youngsters to lie about their age so they can get the papers to stay in the country legally. Many, though, cannot get the necessary papers because they do not carry documentation or have adults who can vouch for who they are and where they come from. So, they wander the streets, begging for money. The younger ones like Brian are picked up by police and housed in a safe place until authorities and aid agencies can figure out what to do with them. While they wait for a future that never seems to arrive, boys like Brian and Temashi -- a legacy of Mugabe's regime -- struggle to survive in the world they now find themselves in.

(CNN) — A crudely carved swastika marks Brian’s arm. The 11-year-old said his friend Temashi, 10, created the menacing image by using a matchstick to “scratch” it into his skin over two days. According to Brian, the process caused only a little pain.

Brian is among thousands of Zimbabwean children who have escaped their devastated country in the hope of finding a better life in South Africa. To him and Temashi, the swastika is not associated with Hitler or the atrocities of the Holocaust. They believe the angular symbol on their arms means “Germans never surrender.”

Although that understanding is distorted and mistaken, Brian said the tattoo gives him courage. Speaking softly, he explained that it identifies him as a “man” and as “someone who does not surrender.” Watch the boys describe what the tattoos signify to them » .

Brian and the other young Zimbabweans are alone in an unfamiliar country. Organizations including UNICEF and Save the Children call them “unaccompanied minors,” but the term barely conveys the reality they face.

Traveling either entirely alone or in small groups of friends, the children undergo extraordinary hardship on their way to South Africa. They catch rides on trucks, trains and taxis. Brian and his companions told CNN that officials at the Beitbridge border crossing allowed them to enter South Africa on foot even though they had neither passports nor other documents.

From there, they traveled to Musina, a town near the border. Boys there beg in the streets or find jobs on farms, while girls appear to vanish into the wider South African population. Shantha Bloemen, a UNICEF representative, said many Zimbabwean girls end up in prostitution or become domestic workers.

Almost all these children—some of whom are not yet 10—leave Zimbabwe believing conditions will improve once they reach South Africa. They cited hunger, poverty and schools that no longer function as reasons for departing. Many have lost their parents; others still have parents. All, however, expressed opposition to the government of Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, whose rule, they said, has given them little alternative but to leave home and join the migration southward.

Humanitarian organizations estimate that one-fourth of Zimbabwe’s population has left the country, with most fleeing to neighboring South Africa, Botswana and Mozambique.

The United Nations and Save the Children, which operates an office in Musina, have documented an alarming rise in the number of people under 18 making the dangerous trip from Zimbabwe to South Africa in search of food and employment. UNICEF and Save the Children social workers told CNN that 175 Zimbabwean children crossed the border illegally and without adults in June. By November, 1,016 children had undertaken the same hazardous journey.

Boys over 16 often remain around Musina, sleeping on pavement near a sports stadium beside older homeless men. During the day, they stand in line and compete for space with hundreds of Zimbabwean adults seeking political asylum at a temporary processing center established by the South African government.

One South African asylum official said young applicants frequently claim to be older than they really are so they can obtain documents allowing them to remain legally in the country. Many are unable to secure those papers, however, because they have no identification and no adults who can confirm their identities or places of origin. As a result, they roam the streets and ask passersby for money.

Police collect younger children such as Brian and place them in a safe facility while government officials and relief organizations decide what should happen to them.

As they wait for a future that always seems out of reach, children like Brian and Temashi—part of the legacy of Mugabe’s government—must fight to stay alive in the unfamiliar circumstances in which they now live.

outputs.L4:
Zimbabwe’s prolonged economic and political crisis has driven growing numbers of children to leave the country without parents or guardians and cross into neighboring South Africa. Interviews conducted by CNN with young migrants and humanitarian organizations portray children fleeing severe hunger, deep poverty, failing schools, and the wider instability that has disrupted everyday life across Zimbabwe. For many, migration is not a choice so much as a desperate attempt to find food, income, education, or safety.

The journey itself exposes the children to grave dangers. Traveling alone or in small groups, some cross borders through unofficial routes, where they risk injury, robbery, exploitation, arrest, and abuse. Without money, documents, or adult protection, they are especially vulnerable to traffickers and others who may take advantage of their desperation.

Reaching South Africa does not necessarily bring security. Unable to obtain regular work or access reliable support, many children survive by begging or accepting poorly paid jobs on farms and in private homes. Others are pushed into prostitution or similarly exploitative situations in exchange for food, shelter, or money. Their undocumented status and fear of authorities can make it difficult for them to report abuse or seek medical care and legal protection.

Aid organizations warn that these unaccompanied minors face malnutrition, homelessness, violence, sexual exploitation, and lasting psychological trauma. Although humanitarian groups provide food, temporary shelter, counseling, and help reconnecting children with their families, their resources are limited and the number of vulnerable migrants remains substantial.

The children’s experiences reveal the human cost of Zimbabwe’s collapse. Economic deprivation, political turmoil, and the breakdown of basic services have not only uprooted families but also forced some of the country’s youngest citizens to take extraordinary risks simply to survive. Their stories underscore the need for stronger child-protection systems, humanitarian assistance, safe access to education, and broader action to address the conditions driving them from home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about unaccompanied Zimbabwean children fleeing poverty and political turmoil for South Africa, focusing on an 11-year-old boy named Brian with a homemade swastika tattoo.
counterfactuals.output:
**Children Alone: Zimbabwe’s Young Migrants Risk Everything to Reach South Africa**

**MUSINA, South Africa** — At 11 years old, Brian has already crossed a border without his parents, slept outdoors and learned to hide from men who prey on children traveling alone.

On his forearm is a crude swastika, scratched into the skin with a needle and darkened with homemade ink. Brian says another boy drew it for him. He did not know its history as the emblem of Nazi Germany or its association with antisemitism and mass murder.

“I thought it would make me look strong,” he says quietly, pulling down his sleeve.

His last name is being withheld to protect his identity.

Brian is among the unaccompanied Zimbabwean children making the dangerous journey south in search of food, work and safety. Aid workers near the border say children arrive exhausted and hungry, some after evading official crossings and navigating stretches of bushland where they face robbery, trafficking, sexual violence and attacks by wild animals.

Zimbabwe has endured years of economic hardship, high unemployment and political instability. For families struggling to afford food, school fees and transportation, South Africa can appear to offer a lifeline — even when reaching it means sending a child into the unknown.

Brian says he left home after meals became increasingly scarce. His mother could not find steady work, he says, and there was no money for school supplies. He traveled with older boys, walking for long periods and relying on strangers for food and water.

At night, he says, fear kept him awake.

“I was thinking about my mother,” Brian says. “I wanted to go back, but I also wanted to continue.”

South Africa is the continent’s most industrialized economy and has long attracted migrants from neighboring countries. But life after crossing the border is often far from the future children imagine. Without documents or adult guardians, minors can struggle to enter school, receive health care or find safe accommodation. Some end up begging, doing informal labor or sleeping in abandoned buildings.

Under both South African law and international child-protection standards, unaccompanied minors should be identified and placed in appropriate care. In practice, humanitarian groups say overwhelmed systems, fear of deportation and a lack of documentation can leave children outside official protection.

“These children are not simply migrants; they are children first,” one local aid worker says. “They need shelter, family tracing, education and psychological support. They should never be treated as criminals.”

Brian’s tattoo has made him stand out among the children at a temporary shelter. Counselors say it is important not to define him by a symbol he did not understand. To them, the mark reflects something deeper: a child trying to create an image of toughness after being made vulnerable by circumstances beyond his control.

They have begun explaining what the symbol means and why it causes pain. Brian now says he wants it removed or covered.

For the moment, his future remains uncertain. Social workers are trying to contact his family and determine whether he can return home safely. Brian says he misses his mother, his friends and the classroom he left behind.

Asked what he wants most, he does not mention money or South Africa.

“I want to go to school,” he says. “And I want to be with my family.”

Around him, other children wait for the same things: a safe bed, a meal and news from home. Their journeys may have crossed an international border, but aid workers say the forces pushing them onto the road — hunger, insecurity and the collapse of opportunity — begin long before they reach it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed humanitarian feature on Zimbabwean minors crossing the border at Beitbridge and surviving on the streets of Musina, using statistics and comments from UNICEF and Save the Children.
counterfactuals.output:
## Between the Limpopo and the Pavement: Zimbabwe’s Children on the Streets of Musina

*Driven by hunger, family separation and economic hardship, Zimbabwean children are making hazardous journeys across the border into South Africa. Reaching Musina offers no guarantee of safety: many face homelessness, exploitation and the constant threat of arrest or deportation.*

**MUSINA, South Africa —** At dawn, the pavements near Musina’s transport ranks begin to stir. Informal traders unpack their goods, taxis fill with passengers, and groups of young Zimbabweans look for casual work carrying bags, washing vehicles or helping vendors.

Among them are children.

Some crossed legally through the Beitbridge border post. Others entered South Africa through gaps in the fence or by wading across the Limpopo River, sometimes following adult smugglers known locally as *magumaguma*. A number arrived with relatives who later disappeared. Others travelled alone from the start.

For these children, Musina—the first major South African town south of the border—is both a destination and a place of limbo. Without money, documents or dependable adults, they may sleep outside shops, in abandoned buildings, near transport depots or in overcrowded rooms shared with strangers.

Their reasons for leaving Zimbabwe vary. Some are trying to reunite with parents already working in South Africa. Others hope to find employment, pay school fees or send food home. Drought, rising prices, unemployment and the erosion of household incomes have also increased pressure on families.

The journey, however, can expose children to robbery, assault, trafficking, sexual violence and drowning. The risks do not end after they cross the border.

### A wider crisis affecting children

UNICEF estimated in its **2024 humanitarian planning for Zimbabwe** that approximately **3.5 million people, including about 1.7 million children, required humanitarian assistance**. The agency linked children’s vulnerability to overlapping pressures including food insecurity, disease outbreaks, inadequate access to water and sanitation, and economic hardship.

Those figures do not measure the number of children crossing at Beitbridge. Reliable border statistics are difficult to obtain because many children use irregular routes, may hide their ages or are recorded as accompanying unrelated adults. But the humanitarian conditions identified by UNICEF help explain why some families see migration—even dangerous migration—as a survival strategy.

Globally, UNICEF estimates that **35.5 million children were living outside their country of birth in 2020**. The agency has repeatedly warned that children travelling without parents or caregivers face heightened risks of violence, trafficking, exploitation and family separation.

Save the Children has also warned that Zimbabwe’s economic and climate-related emergencies are having a disproportionate effect on children. In its public advocacy on child migration, the organisation stresses that poverty, hunger and lack of schooling can push children into unsafe movement and hazardous work, while restrictive border policies can force them toward smugglers and more dangerous routes.

Both UNICEF and Save the Children maintain that a child’s immigration status should never override the child’s rights. Their guidance calls for unaccompanied and separated children to be identified quickly, placed in safe care, given access to health services and education, and supported through family tracing and a formal assessment of their best interests.

### Crossing through danger

Beitbridge is one of southern Africa’s busiest land borders. The official post sits beside a much less regulated landscape of bush paths, farms and river crossings.

During the dry season, sections of the Limpopo may appear shallow enough to cross on foot. Sudden channels, soft mud and deep pools remain dangerous. In the rainy season, fast-moving water can be deadly. Children also report fears of crocodiles, snakes, criminals and security patrols.

The use of smugglers creates another layer of risk. A child who cannot pay an agreed fee may be abandoned, robbed or forced to work. Girls are particularly vulnerable to sexual exploitation, although boys can also face abuse, coercion and trafficking.

Children frequently travel without proof of age, birth certificates or passports. Some avoid authorities because they fear detention or deportation. That fear can make them reluctant to seek help even after violence or illness.

UNICEF’s position is that immigration detention is never in a child’s best interests and that children should instead receive community-based care and protection. The agency also argues that border authorities must presume a person is a child when age is uncertain until an appropriate, child-sensitive assessment is completed.

### Survival in Musina

Once in Musina, children need immediate necessities: food, water, a safe place to sleep and protection from adults who may exploit them. Yet survival often depends on informal work.

A child may earn a few rand by pushing a trolley, loading luggage or cleaning a vehicle. Others collect recyclable materials or ask travellers for food. The income is unreliable and the work can expose children to injury, wage theft and harassment.

Sleeping outside intensifies these dangers. Children may form small groups for protection, but street-based networks are not a substitute for trained caregivers. Older youths or adults can control sleeping spaces and access to work. Substance use may become a means of coping with hunger, cold, fear or trauma.

Girls on the move can be less visible because they are more likely to be absorbed into private homes, domestic work or exploitative relationships. Their absence from the street does not necessarily mean they are safe. A child living behind a closed door may be harder for social workers to identify and assist.

Save the Children’s child-protection guidance emphasises that unaccompanied children should not be treated simply as undocumented migrants. They are children first and must be screened for abuse, trafficking, disability, illness and family-separation concerns. The organisation has also called for children’s cases to be handled individually rather than through mass deportations.

### The legal and protection gap

South Africa’s child-protection laws apply to every child in the country, regardless of nationality or documentation. In principle, a child found without parental care should be referred to social workers and placed in appropriate care.

In practice, frontline services can be overstretched. Establishing a child’s identity may take time, especially when records are missing or when relatives are scattered between Zimbabwe and South Africa. Shelters must also balance urgent demand with limited beds, staffing and funding.

Repatriation is not as simple as putting a child on a bus to the border. International child-protection standards require family tracing, verification that the receiving caregiver is appropriate and an assessment of whether return is safe and in the child’s best interests.

Returning a child without those safeguards can restart the same cycle. If hunger, abuse or family separation remains unresolved, the child may attempt the crossing again—this time using a more concealed and dangerous route.

UNICEF advocates cross-border case management so that social workers, immigration officials and child-protection agencies in both countries can share information safely and maintain support after a child returns. Save the Children similarly promotes coordinated family tracing and reintegration assistance, including access to education, food and livelihoods for the household receiving the child.

### Education interrupted

Migration often follows months or years of interrupted schooling. Once children are in Musina, lack of documents, frequent movement and the pressure to earn money can make returning to a classroom difficult.

Yet education is one of the strongest protective measures available. A child attending school is more visible to teachers and social workers, more likely to receive regular support and less exposed to hazardous labour.

UNICEF and Save the Children both argue that migrant and refugee children should have access to education irrespective of status. Temporary learning programmes can help, but they should lead toward inclusion in formal schooling rather than become a permanent parallel system.

For adolescents, education must also be paired with realistic livelihood support. A teenager who is the main source of income for younger siblings cannot simply be told to stop working. Safe skills training, cash assistance and support for the wider family may be needed to remove the economic pressure driving the child onto the street.

### More than a border problem

The presence of Zimbabwean children on Musina’s streets is often framed as an immigration-control issue. Humanitarian agencies argue that it is fundamentally a child-protection issue—and one that cannot be solved at the border alone.

Stronger patrols may change the routes children use, but they do not eliminate the reasons they leave. Without safe migration channels and social support, tougher enforcement can push children deeper into the bush and increase their dependence on smugglers.

A durable response would require Zimbabwe and South Africa to expand cross-border child-protection teams, improve age-appropriate screening at Beitbridge, fund shelters and social workers in Musina, and ensure that no child is returned without an individual assessment and verified reception plan.

It would also require investment in the communities children leave behind: food assistance, drought response, schools, family livelihoods and protection from abuse.

Until those pressures ease, Musina will continue to be both refuge and hazard. The town’s streets may offer a child a meal or a day’s work, but they cannot provide the safety, education and stable care to which every child is entitled.

For a minor who has already survived the river, the smugglers and the long road south, crossing the border is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of another struggle—to remain visible as a child, rather than being treated only as a migrant.

*Note: Humanitarian needs and migration figures change rapidly. Before publication, the Zimbabwe-specific UNICEF figures should be checked against the latest UNICEF Humanitarian Action for Children appeal, and local operational data and comments should be confirmed with UNICEF Zimbabwe/South Africa and Save the Children’s regional offices.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an early-2000s-style CNN article explaining why young Zimbabwean migrants Brian and Temashi interpret their scratched swastika tattoos as symbols of strength rather than Nazism.
counterfactuals.output:
## Young migrants see strength in symbol scarred by history

**HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) —** Scratched into the skin of Brian and Temashi are crude swastikas — symbols that, in much of the world, immediately evoke Adolf Hitler, Nazi Germany and the Holocaust.

But the young Zimbabwean migrants say that is not what the tattoos mean to them.

Made by hand with improvised needles and ink, the marks were intended as signs of toughness and survival, they say — permanent reminders of the hardships they endured while moving far from home.

“To us, it means being strong,” Brian said, tracing the uneven lines on his arm. “It means nobody can break you.”

Temashi offered a similar explanation. The pair encountered the design not through books about Nazi Europe, they said, but among other young men who treated it as a badge of fearlessness. Removed from its historical setting, the symbol became part of a visual language of bravado and belonging.

The swastika is far older than Nazism. For thousands of years, versions of it appeared in Hindu, Buddhist and other cultures, often representing good fortune, well-being or the movement of the sun.

But Hitler’s Nazi Party adopted the symbol in the 20th century, transforming it into an emblem of racial hatred. Under the swastika banner, Nazi Germany murdered 6 million Jews and millions of other victims during the Holocaust.

Historians say that legacy makes the symbol deeply offensive and threatening, regardless of the wearer’s intentions.

Brian and Temashi say they knew little of that history when they marked themselves. Their tattoos were not declarations of white supremacy, they insist, but products of migration, isolation and a youth culture in which powerful images are frequently borrowed without understanding their origins.

The roughness of the tattoos is part of their meaning. Unlike professional body art, they were scratched into the skin in difficult circumstances, turning pain itself into a test of endurance.

Yet the young men’s explanation does not erase the symbol’s impact. To survivors of Nazi persecution and many others, a swastika cannot easily be separated from genocide.

That gap — between intended meaning and received meaning — leaves Brian and Temashi carrying a sign whose history is much larger than their own. To them, it records resilience. To much of the world, it represents terror.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the growing number of children fleeing Robert Mugabe’s Zimbabwe alone in search of food and work in South Africa. Include their dangerous journeys, asylum difficulties, exploitation risks, and living conditions.
counterfactuals.output:
## Zimbabwe’s child exodus to South Africa

During the worst years of Robert Mugabe’s rule, Zimbabwe’s economic collapse drove a growing number of children to leave the country without parents or guardians. Many travelled to South Africa hoping to find food, casual work and money for relatives at home. The movement was difficult to quantify because many children crossed the border clandestinely and avoided officials, but aid agencies reported increasing numbers of unaccompanied minors in towns near the border.

### Dangerous journeys

Children—some in their early teens or younger—often walked or used informal transport to reach the Limpopo River. Those without passports crossed through the bush or paid smugglers known as *malaicha* to guide them.

The journey exposed them to:

- drowning or crocodile attacks while crossing the Limpopo;
- dehydration, hunger and extreme temperatures;
- robbery, assault and rape;
- demands for additional money from smugglers;
- exploitation by criminal gangs and corrupt officials;
- arrest and deportation by South African authorities.

Girls were especially vulnerable to sexual violence and trafficking, while boys were sometimes forced to carry goods, surrender their possessions or work to repay transport fees.

### Barriers to asylum and protection

Although unaccompanied children should be treated primarily as children in need of protection, many struggled to enter South Africa’s asylum system. Some did not understand the process, lacked identity papers or feared that approaching police or immigration officials would lead to detention and deportation. Younger children could not always explain where they had come from or locate relatives.

Zimbabweans fleeing hunger and economic breakdown also faced a legal problem: poverty alone did not necessarily meet the formal definition of a refugee. Yet economic hardship was intertwined with political repression, the destruction of livelihoods and the collapse of public services. Asylum offices were overcrowded, and children often lacked adults able to help them complete applications or attend interviews.

As a result, many remained undocumented. This restricted their access to schooling, health care, shelters and lawful employment, despite South African constitutional and child-protection guarantees that apply regardless of nationality.

### Exploitation and child labour

Without papers or family support, children depended on informal work. In border areas and cities, they washed cars, carried goods, collected scrap, sold small items, worked on farms or performed domestic labour. Employers could pay them very little—or nothing—because the children were unlikely to complain.

Others were drawn into begging, theft, smuggling or commercial sexual exploitation. Children sleeping outdoors were particularly vulnerable to trafficking and abuse by adults who offered transport, employment or accommodation. Fear of arrest made it harder for them to report violence.

### Living conditions

Many unaccompanied children lived in overcrowded shelters, abandoned buildings, informal settlements or on the streets in places such as Musina and Johannesburg. They frequently lacked regular meals, clean water, sanitation and medical care. Shelters near the border were often overwhelmed and could provide only temporary accommodation.

Education was disrupted or ended altogether. Even where schools were legally required to admit migrant children, missing documents, fees, uniforms, language barriers and frequent movement kept many out of classrooms. Isolation and uncertainty also took a psychological toll: children worried about relatives in Zimbabwe while coping with violence, hunger and life without trusted adults.

### A protection crisis

The exodus reflected more than ordinary labour migration. Zimbabwe’s hyperinflation, food shortages, unemployment, political violence and failing schools and hospitals pushed children into adult responsibilities. South Africa offered the possibility of food and income, but irregular migration left them exposed to a different set of dangers.

Humanitarian organizations urged authorities to identify unaccompanied minors at the border, appoint guardians, provide safe accommodation and family tracing, and assess each child’s best interests before any return to Zimbabwe. They also called for access to documentation, education and health care, together with stronger action against trafficking and abusive employers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a long-form news story beginning with a vivid description of Brian’s arm tattoo, then broaden the narrative to examine the plight of undocumented Zimbabwean child migrants in South Africa.
counterfactuals.output:
*Editor’s note: Brian is a pseudonym used to protect the identity of a minor.*

## Marked by the Journey: Zimbabwe’s Undocumented Children in South Africa

The tattoo begins just below Brian’s right elbow: three uneven blue lines, blurred at the edges, running toward his wrist like a road drawn from memory.

A small cross sits at one end. At the other is a crude letter **B**, pressed into the skin with a needle and ink when he was 15. Between them, faint beneath the shine of scar tissue, is the outline of a bird.

Brian rolls down his sleeve whenever police officers pass.

To anyone else, the tattoo might look like the impulsive work of a teenager. To Brian, now 17, it is a map of what he has lost. The cross is for his mother, who died in Zimbabwe. The bird represents the border he crossed into South Africa. The three lines stand for the three boys who began the journey with him.

Only two arrived.

Brian does not know what happened to the third.

“He went back with the men,” Brian says quietly, referring to the smugglers who guided them through the bush near the Limpopo River. “Maybe he was caught. Maybe he is home.”

Brian has no passport, no birth certificate in his possession and no document proving that he has a legal right to remain in South Africa. He sleeps in a crowded room in central Johannesburg with other young Zimbabweans, taking casual work where he can find it—carrying boxes, washing vehicles, unloading vegetables before dawn.

He is one of an unknown number of undocumented Zimbabwean children living in South Africa, part of a largely invisible migration shaped by economic hardship, family separation, political uncertainty and the belief that opportunity lies south of the border.

No reliable count exists. Undocumented children are, by definition, difficult to track. Some travel with parents or relatives. Others cross alone, moving through unofficial routes where they face robbery, extortion, sexual violence, trafficking, injury and drowning. Once inside South Africa, many disappear into farms, border towns and major cities, beyond the reach of both governments and child-protection agencies.

They arrive as children but are often treated first as foreigners.

### A border crossed in darkness

Brian grew up outside Gweru in central Zimbabwe. His father left when he was small, he says, and his mother sold vegetables and second-hand clothes. After she died, he stayed briefly with an aunt whose household was already struggling.

School fees, uniforms and food became impossible expenses.

An older boy told Brian that work was available in Johannesburg. The two boarded buses and shared taxis heading south, joining other travellers near the border town of Beitbridge. Without valid documents, they could not use the official crossing.

They waited until night.

The Limpopo River, which forms part of the boundary between Zimbabwe and South Africa, can appear deceptively shallow in the dry season. During periods of heavy rain, it becomes fast and dangerous. Migrants crossing away from official posts may also encounter criminal groups, armed robbers and smugglers who demand additional payment once a journey has begun.

Brian remembers walking for hours through thorny brush. He remembers being told not to use a phone or speak. He remembers men taking money from one of the boys and beating him when he said he had nothing left.

What he cannot remember clearly is when the missing boy vanished.

The group scattered after someone shouted that police or soldiers were nearby. Brian and another teenager hid under shrubs until morning. When they returned to the meeting point, the boy was gone.

There was no adult to report him missing.

### Rights on paper, barriers in practice

South Africa’s Constitution and child-protection laws provide significant safeguards for children, regardless of nationality or immigration status. The country is also bound by international and regional agreements affirming children’s rights to protection, education and basic services.

In principle, a child should not be denied basic education merely because a parent cannot produce immigration papers. Public health facilities are also expected to provide essential care, particularly emergency treatment and services for children.

In practice, undocumented migrant families frequently encounter confusion, inconsistent rules and demands for papers they do not have.

At schools, parents and guardians may be asked for birth certificates, passports, proof of address or study permits. Some administrators allow children to enrol while documents are being sought. Others turn families away, sometimes because officials misunderstand the law and sometimes because overcrowded schools are searching for any basis to limit admissions.

Unaccompanied children face even greater obstacles. They may have no parent to sign forms, no official guardian, no previous school records and no safe address. A teenager who has missed several years of schooling may also be too old for the grade matching his educational level.

Brian tried once to return to school in Johannesburg.

He says a man from his building took him to a nearby secondary school. They were told to bring identification and records from Zimbabwe. Brian had neither. He did not go back.

Now he can read basic English, but slowly. He counts money carefully and uses the calculator on a borrowed phone for larger amounts. When employers underpay him, he rarely argues.

Without documents, he fears that any dispute could draw the attention of police or immigration officials.

### Children hiding in plain sight

On Johannesburg’s streets, adolescent migrants can look older than they are. Boys carry loads at markets, work on construction sites or collect recyclable material. Girls may clean homes, care for children or sell goods informally. Some children live with extended family members; others depend on unrelated adults who offer shelter in exchange for work.

That dependence creates opportunities for exploitation.

An employer can withhold wages. A landlord can threaten eviction. An adult can demand sex, labour or money while reminding the child that reporting abuse could lead to arrest or deportation.

For girls, the risks are often especially hidden. Some migrate after being promised domestic work, only to find themselves confined in private homes. Others enter relationships with older partners because they need rent, food or protection. Pregnancy can deepen their vulnerability, especially if they fear seeking medical care.

Boys are more visible in public spaces and more likely to be swept up in police operations, but visibility does not necessarily bring protection. A child without papers may be presumed to be an adult migrant. Age assessments can be difficult when no birth certificate exists, and teenagers themselves may claim to be older because they believe adulthood will help them find work.

The result is a dangerous contradiction: children sometimes hide their age to survive, then lose access to the protections attached to childhood.

### The documentation trap

Obtaining papers can become a circular process.

To apply for one document, a family may be asked to produce another. A birth certificate may require evidence from parents who are missing, deceased or undocumented themselves. Records may be held in Zimbabwe, far from the child and costly to retrieve. Names and birth dates can be recorded differently across school, clinic and immigration files.

Some children were born in South Africa to Zimbabwean parents but remain undocumented because their births were not registered promptly or because their parents lacked the required paperwork. Being born in South Africa does not automatically make a child a citizen, and those without proof of another nationality can face years of uncertainty.

Older Zimbabwean migrants have also lived through repeated changes in permit systems and immigration policy. Adults may lose legal status when permits expire, applications fail or administrative deadlines pass. When parents become undocumented, their children’s access to stable schooling, housing and healthcare can become more precarious as well.

Fear compounds the problem. Families may avoid government offices because they worry their information could be shared with immigration enforcement authorities. Even when that fear is based on rumour rather than official policy, it can be powerful enough to keep a sick child away from a clinic or an eligible pupil out of school.

### Hostility in the communities they enter

South Africa has long been a destination for migrants from across the continent, while also struggling with high unemployment, inequality and pressure on public services. During periods of tension, foreign nationals are blamed for joblessness, crime or overcrowding.

Zimbabweans, Mozambicans, Malawians, Congolese, Somalis and other migrants have faced harassment, attacks and displacement during repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence.

Children absorb that hostility early.

Zimbabwean pupils sometimes attempt to change their accents or avoid speaking Shona and Ndebele in public. Some use South African names. Others conceal where they were born, fearful that classmates will call them *makwerekwere*, a derogatory term for African foreigners.

For undocumented children, bullying carries an additional threat: exposure.

A schoolyard argument can become a taunt about deportation. A neighbour can report a family after a dispute. A young worker who asks for unpaid wages can be told that the police will be called.

This atmosphere encourages silence, and silence makes abuse harder to detect.

### A system divided between protection and control

Undocumented child migration falls between agencies with different responsibilities. Immigration authorities are mandated to enforce national borders. Social workers must act in the best interests of children. Police investigate crime but may also participate in immigration operations. Schools and clinics provide services while navigating administrative requirements.

When these systems do not coordinate, children can be lost between them.

A child intercepted near the border may need emergency care, family tracing, an assessment of trafficking risks and a safe placement. Returning that child to Zimbabwe without understanding why he or she left could place the child back in danger. Yet keeping a child in South Africa without documentation, schooling or family support can also prolong instability.

Child-rights advocates have argued that decisions should be made individually and that deportation should never be an automatic response to an undocumented child. The central question, they say, should be what serves the child’s best interests—not simply how the child crossed the border.

But such assessments require trained staff, time and functioning cross-border cooperation. Social-service systems in both countries are under pressure, and shelters often lack space. Older adolescents can be particularly difficult to place because facilities may prioritise younger children and teenagers may resist institutional care.

Many leave shelters or temporary accommodation and return to informal work.

### Growing up without proof

Brian turns 18 later this year—or at least he believes he does.

His exact birth date is uncertain. His mother told him he was born near the end of the rainy season. A school record in Zimbabwe may contain the date, but Brian does not know how to obtain it. He no longer has his aunt’s phone number.

Adulthood will not resolve his legal status. It may instead remove the limited protections available to him as a child.

He hopes to become a mechanic. When cars stop beside the pavement where he waits for work, he studies their engines. He has learned to change tyres and oil, and he sometimes helps a mechanic who pays him in cash.

Yet training programmes generally require identification. Formal employers require documents. Opening a bank account, signing a lease or registering a mobile number can become difficult. Each ordinary step into adult life leads back to the same missing papers.

For now, Brian keeps his belongings in a plastic shopping bag: two shirts, a pair of trousers, a phone charger and a small photograph of his mother. The photograph is creased through the middle. He does not carry it to work because he fears losing it.

The tattoo is different. It cannot be stolen.

In the late afternoon, as commuters move through Johannesburg’s crowded streets, Brian pushes his sleeve above his elbow and looks again at the faded bird. The ink has spread since the night he pressed it into his skin. Its wings are no longer even.

He traces the three blue lines with one finger.

They mark a journey across a national border, but also a more difficult passage: from childhood into an adulthood without records, certainty or legal belonging. Around him are thousands of people moving with identity cards in wallets, names on databases and addresses they can prove.

Brian carries his proof on his arm.

Then a police van turns into the street.

He pulls down his sleeve and disappears into the crowd.
